About

About me

Hi, I'm Yashraj — a computational physicist at Princeton University working at the intersection of molecular simulations and machine learning. My research centers on how the fundamental building blocks of life — proteins, RNA, and DNA — self-organize inside cells, and what shapes their internal structure and transport.

Biology is in the middle of a remarkable technological moment, where advances in computing and data are letting us ask questions about cells that were simply out of reach a decade ago. I'm interested in using this moment well: combining ML with molecular simulations to understand how biomolecules assemble into functional structures, what goes wrong when they don't, and whether we can design interventions to correct it.

Outside the lab, I play chess and badminton. If you want to talk science, explore a collaboration, or just say hello — I'd love to hear from you.

Research

Publications

  • Non-equilibrium modeling of flux through biomolecular condensates
    Wani YM, Joseph JA
    bioRxiv 2026  —  Preprint

    Biomolecular condensates like the nucleolus and stress granules function out of equilibrium, sustained by the continuous flux of molecular components. We introduce TRACE (TRansport Across Condensate Environments), a coarse-grained simulation framework that maintains a non-equilibrium steady-state concentration gradient to directly quantify molecular flux at residue-level resolution. Using TRACE, we show that protein sequence composition and patterning dictate the condensate's internal pore architecture — the primary determinant of transport efficiency. Guest molecule stiffness enhances flux, host–guest interactions jointly tune solubility and diffusivity, and crosslinking shrinks pore size and hinders transport, consistent with experimental observations of dextran diffusion through nuclear phases.

  • Tuning the morphology and structure of supraparticles composed of ellipsoids
    Yetkin M, Wani YM, Nikoubashman A, Butt HJ, Kappl M
    Langmuir 41 (11), 7845–7855. 2025

    When colloidal dispersions evaporate on superamphiphobic surfaces, they self-assemble into micron-scale supraparticles whose shape and internal structure depend sensitively on the building blocks used. We show that supraparticles composed of polystyrene ellipsoids (aspect ratios 4–11) adopt a buckled, irregular morphology by default, but become spherical upon addition of the surfactant SDS, which stabilizes the colloids during drying. At low Péclet numbers (slow evaporation), the ellipsoids order into nematic bundles inside the supraparticle and into smectic-like domains on its surface — a structural richness absent in sphere-based supraparticles. In binary sphere–ellipsoid mixtures, even low concentrations of spheres disrupt this orientational ordering, revealing a handle for tuning both morphology and internal architecture.

  • Exploring the role of hydrodynamic interactions in spherically confined drying colloidal suspensions
    Kundu M, Kritika K, Wani YM, Nikoubashman A, Howard MP
    The Journal of Chemical Physics 162 (15). 2025

    When a colloidal suspension dries inside a spherical freestanding droplet, particles accumulate near the liquid–vapor interface — but the extent of this stratification depends critically on how solvent-mediated forces are modeled. Using both dynamic density functional theory (DDFT) and particle-based simulations (Brownian dynamics and multiparticle collision dynamics), we show that pairwise hydrodynamic interactions (HIs) between colloids significantly amplify the concentration gradients that build up during drying compared to the free-draining approximation, while solvent boundary conditions at the droplet surface have little effect. We further find that DDFT, which performs well under free-draining conditions, breaks down when pairwise HIs are included — erroneously ejecting particles from the droplet as concentrations rise. We trace this failure to an inaccurate approximation of two-body density correlations based on bulk pair functions, and support this diagnosis with confined equilibrium correlation data from particle-based simulations.

  • Mesoscale simulations of diffusion and sedimentation in shape-anisotropic nanoparticle suspensions
    Wani YM†, Kovakas PG†, Nikoubashman A, Howard MP (†equal contribution)
    Soft Matter 20 (19), 3942–3953. 2024

    How do nanoparticles diffuse and settle when their shape departs from a simple sphere? Using multiparticle collision dynamics (MPCD) — a mesoscale method that explicitly captures solvent-mediated hydrodynamic interactions — we compute the long-time self-diffusion and sedimentation coefficients for suspensions of four anisotropic shapes: octahedra, cubes, tetrahedra, and spherocylinders, across a range of concentrations. Simulations agree well with existing theoretical predictions and experimental data. A key practical finding: for regular polyhedral shapes, the diffusion coefficient can be accurately estimated from the equivalent-sphere result using a diameter equal to the average of the inscribed and circumscribed sphere diameters — a simple rule of thumb that bypasses expensive shape-specific calculations.

  • Structure formation in supraparticles composed of spherical and elongated particles
    Yetkin M†, Wani YM†, Kritika K, Howard MP, Kappl M, Butt HJ, Nikoubashman A (†equal contribution)
    Langmuir 40 (1), 1096–1108. 2024

    Aqueous droplets containing dispersions of ellipsoidal polystyrene particles — alone or mixed with spheres — were dried on superamphiphobic surfaces at different humidity levels to vary the evaporation rate. Pure-ellipsoid droplets consistently produce supraparticles with short-range lateral ordering at the surface and random orientations in the interior, regardless of evaporation rate. Particle-based simulations confirm this picture in the evaporation-limited regime and show increasing nematic order as the diffusion-limited regime is reached. When ellipsoids are mixed with spheres, a thin shell of ellipsoids forms at the supraparticle surface, while porosity increases with ellipsoid aspect ratio. Together, the experiments and simulations reveal how evaporation rate, particle shape, and composition jointly control supraparticle architecture.

  • Coarse-grained simulations of columnar ionic liquid crystals: comparison with experiments
    Kolmangadi MA#, Wani YM#, Schönhals A, Nikoubashman A (#equal contribution)
    The Journal of Physical Chemistry B 128 (34), 8215–8222. 2024

    Guanidinium-based columnar ionic liquid crystals (ILCs) combine ionic conductivity with liquid-crystalline order, but the molecular basis of their mesophase behavior remains poorly understood. Using coarse-grained Martini force field simulations, we study a homologous series of ILCs with alkyl side chains of length n = 8, 12, and 16, and compare directly with experimental data. Short-chain ILC-8 forms a percolated network with weak columnar order, while ILC-12 and ILC-16 self-assemble into well-defined hexagonally ordered columns — a transition that mirrors the experimentally observed broadening of the mesophase window with chain length. The intercolumnar spacing increases with chain length and decreases with temperature, in quantitative agreement with X-ray data. Diffusion coefficients and ionic conductivity drop sharply with chain length, which we attribute to the formation of ordered columns that restrict ion mobility more than percolated networks do.

  • Diffusion and sedimentation in colloidal suspensions using multiparticle collision dynamics with a discrete particle model
    Wani YM, Kovakas PG, Nikoubashman A, Howard MP
    The Journal of Chemical Physics 156 (2). 2022

    Accurately capturing hydrodynamic interactions between colloidal particles demands resolving the solvent, but fully atomistic approaches quickly become prohibitive. We introduce a hybrid scheme — MD+MPCD — that couples a multiparticle collision dynamics (MPCD) solvent with a discrete mesh model for the colloidal particles, capturing both translational and rotational hydrodynamic coupling efficiently. Benchmarking against experiments and Brownian dynamics with the Rotne–Prager–Yamakawa mobility tensor across volume fractions from 0.01 to 0.40, we find that the long-time self-diffusion and sedimentation coefficients from MD+MPCD agree well with experimental data, despite partial coupling between particle and solvent at short times. We further demonstrate the method's versatility by computing the self-diffusion coefficient for suspensions of nearly hard cubes, where analytic mobility tensors are unavailable.
